*Code covered: the model-loading part of `tools/traduire_paragraphes.py`.*

## The joint: one function, one signature

The whole translation pipeline rests on a one-line contract:

```python
translate(texts: list[str]) -> list[str]
```

As many outputs as inputs, in the same order. Nothing else. Each translator supplies its
own implementation, and the rest of the code — segmentation, protection, loop, CSV
writing — does not know which one is running.

That is what makes it possible to add a translator by writing one single function, and
it is why swapping translators never touched anything else: the joint sits exactly on
the boundary between what depends on the model and what does not.

## The three models

| | HPLT | TranslateGemma | MiLMMT-46 |
|---|---|---|---|
| checkpoint | `HPLT/translate-en-hr-v1.0-hplt_opus` | `google/translategemma-27b-it` | `xiaomi-research/MiLMMT-46-12B-v1.0` |
| architecture | Marian, encoder-decoder | Gemma 3, multimodal | Gemma 3, decoder-only |
| parameters | 77 M | 27 B | 12 B |
| weights in bf16 | 0.15 GB | 55 GB | 24 GB |
| context | **512 tokens** (hard limit) | 2,048 tokens (model card) | 131,072 (architecture) |
| prompt shape | none, raw text | multimodal message template | text completion |
| `transformers` | **4.26 – 4.30** | >= 4.50 | >= 4.50 |

Three technically unrelated families, reduced to the same contract. Only MiLMMT-46 is
loaded by the pipeline as it stands; the other two are here because the comparison is
what selected it.

::: {.callout-important}
## Each translator runs at *its own* window

The temptation, when comparing three translators, is to cap them all at the most
constrained one — here HPLT and its 512 tokens — so that the comparison is "fair".

That would be a protocol error, because **the intended comparison is not between
translators**. Each translation is compared against the original English: the question
is "does the extraction survive this move into Croatian?", not "which of the three is
best?". Capping MiLMMT at HPLT's window would degrade the Croatian produced without
teaching anything.

Hence `--max-chars` being a per-translator option rather than a global constant.
:::

In practice HPLT's window constrains almost nobody, for the reason seen in the previous
chapter: the median paragraph is 109 characters in English and 123 in Croatian, i.e.
around forty tokens. The largest paragraph in the corpus (3,304 characters) is the only
case that calls for splitting into sentences.

## MiLMMT: a plain completion

This is the translator that was kept, and the only one the current pipeline loads.

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
montre("load", ou=PARAGRAPHES)
```

No chat template: the prompt is raw text, taken word for word from the model's
documentation.

```{python}
#| echo: false
print("Translate this from English to Croatian:")
print("English: A right internal jugular central venous catheter was placed.")
print("Croatian:")
```

The language labels come from `--src` and `--tgt`, and have to be the ones in the
model's documentation (`English`, `Croatian`, not `en` or `hr`): an unrecognised label
degrades the translation **without raising an error**.

::: {.callout-warning}
## Two traps in batched generation on a decoder

**`padding_side = "left"`.** With right padding, the last position of each short
sequence is a padding token: the model continues *from the padding* rather than from the
end of the prompt. The output stays plausible, so the mistake is invisible.

**Stripping the prompt off the output.** A completion model copies its input at the head
of its generation. `gen[:, enc["input_ids"].shape[1]:]` keeps only what follows — and
left padding makes that slice valid for the whole batch, since every sequence then has
the same input length.

The two points hold together: left padding is what makes the slice simple, and the
simple slice is what makes the batch usable.
:::

## `budget`: the invisible truncation

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
montre("budget", ou=PARAGRAPHES)
```

A fixed `max_new_tokens` is a trap. Set too low, the translation is **cut off
mid-sentence, without an error**: the corpus ends up missing the end of every long
segment, and nothing reports it — no exception, no warning, no counter.

The function therefore computes a ceiling per batch, from the longest segment:

```{python}
#| output: asis
budget = fonction("budget", PARAGRAPHES)
tableau([{"longest segment": f"{n} chars",
          "max_new_tokens": budget(["x" * n])}
         for n in (80, 300, 1200, 3300, 8000)])
```

The constants are measured, not guessed: ~3.5 characters per token, and a factor of
**2.0** of margin because Croatian consumes about 15 % more tokens than English, plus a
reserve for atypical paragraphs. The `+ 64` covers very short paragraphs, where a
multiplicative factor is not enough.

The ceiling bounds the cost: beyond it, translating a single paragraph would monopolise
the GPU. What makes this computation indispensable is developed in "The paragraph, a
universal unit" — a ceiling set too low raises no error, it cuts the end off the text.

## The batch sorted by length, and recursion on OOM {#sec-lots}

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
fichier(PARAGRAPHES, "    def translate(texts: list[str])", "    return translate")
```

**Sorting by length is what makes the batch safe.** Within a batch, every sequence is
padded up to the length of the longest one: a 1,200-character segment forces its 31
neighbours to that size, and the activations overflow. Grouping segments of similar
length removes that waste. The original order is restored at the end through the
`output` dictionary, indexed on the initial position.

The mechanism was written after an incident: an out-of-memory error at `batch_size=64`
in bf16, on a note of 79 segments, discovered two hours after launch. Hence the second
protection — **recursive re-splitting**:

```
batch of 32  --OOM-->  16 + 16  --OOM-->  8 + 8  ...  --OOM on 1 segment--> re-raise
```

An overflow then slows one note down, instead of losing three hours of a run. The
stopping condition (`if len(indices) == 1: raise`) is necessary: a segment that does not
pass on its own never will, and an unguarded recursion would run forever.

## Two Python environments, and why {#sec-venvs}

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
docstring(PARAGRAPHES)
```

The constraint is irreducible: HPLT requires `transformers` 4.26–4.30, Gemma 3 requires
>= 4.50. No single version satisfies both.

| environment | Python | `transformers` | for |
|---|---|---|---|
| `.venv312` | 3.12 | 5.5.0 | TranslateGemma, MiLMMT, extraction |
| `.venv-hplt` | **3.11** | 4.28.1 | HPLT only |
| `.venv-docs` | 3.12 | — | rendering this document |

Python 3.11 for HPLT and not 3.12: `tokenizers` 0.13, forced by `transformers` 4.28, has
no prebuilt wheel for 3.12 and building it from source fails. This is the kind of
cascading constraint better written down once than rediscovered.

Only `.venv312` is needed to run the pipeline as it stands. The other two exist because
the comparison happened, and because this document has to be rendered without loading
torch.

## `main()`: what happens, in what order

Everything above is a piece. `main()` is what assembles them, and its shape is one
deliberate decision: **spend nothing on the GPU until every cheap check has passed.**

### First, three checks that cost no GPU at all

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
fichier(PARAGRAPHES, "    notes = pd.read_csv(ROOT / args.data)", "    out = ROOT / args.out")
```

In order: read the corpus, optionally keep one note in N (`--shard`, one process per
GPU), then **split every note and re-join it without translating** and check that the
`___` count comes back unchanged. That round trip exercises `split`, `sentences` and the
re-joining on the real corpus, in about two seconds, and it fails before a single byte of
model has been downloaded. `plan_vram` then estimates the footprint from `--batch` and
`--max-chars` — also before loading.

The pattern is worth naming: the two checks that could invalidate a run of several hours
both run in the first three seconds.

### Then resume, and only then load the model

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
fichier(PARAGRAPHES, "    out = ROOT / args.out", "    for k, row in enumerate")
```

The output CSV **is** the ledger. Notes whose `id_note` already appears in it are
subtracted; if nothing is left, the function returns *before* `load()` is called. So
relaunching a finished run costs nothing, and relaunching an interrupted one loads the
model only when there is work.

### The batch: what exactly runs in parallel {#sec-lot-quoi}

This is the question the code does not answer on its own. `--batch 24` does not mean 24
notes, and it does not mean 24 characters or 24 sentences. **One element of a batch is one
call, and one call is one paragraph** — 92.2 % of the time. The other 7.8 % are pieces of
a paragraph that exceeded `--max-chars` and was cut on sentence boundaries.

Measured on the 249 English notes, at the defaults:

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
import math, statistics as st
import pandas as pd
# `split` appelle `paragraphs` et `sentences` : fonction() n'injecte que `re`,
# donc on lui passe les deux dépendances explicitement.
paragraphs = fonction("paragraphs", PARAGRAPHES)
sentences = fonction("sentences", PARAGRAPHES)
split = fonction("split", PARAGRAPHES, paragraphs=paragraphs, sentences=sentences)
notes = [str(x) for x in
         pd.read_excel(RACINE / "CATH-LLM" / "exampleNotes_250.xlsx")["input"].dropna()]
calls = [len(split(t, 1000)) for t in notes]
batches = [math.ceil(c / 24) for c in calls]
tableau([
    {"quantity": "paragraphs in a note", "median": int(st.median([len(paragraphs(t)) for t in notes])),
     "max": max(len(paragraphs(t)) for t in notes)},
    {"quantity": "calls in a note", "median": int(st.median(calls)), "max": max(calls)},
    {"quantity": "batches of 24 in a note", "median": int(st.median(batches)), "max": max(batches)},
])
print(f"\n{sum(calls)} calls in {sum(batches)} batches over the 249 notes — "
      f"{sum(1 for b in batches if b == 1)} notes fit in a single batch.")
```

So the answer to "how many paragraphs at once": **up to 24, but never more than the note
itself contains.** `translate()` is called once per note, so a batch never spans two
notes. The median note has 40 calls, which is two batches: one full, one of sixteen.

::: {.callout-note}
## The cost of batching per note

240 of the 249 notes end on an incomplete batch, half full on average. Batching across
note boundaries would recover that, and it is deliberately not done: the resume ledger
works at note granularity, so a batch that spans two notes would make an interruption
ambiguous — one note half written, and no way to say so in the CSV.

Paying about half a batch per note buys an interruption that costs exactly one note. On a
run of several hours, that was the right side of the trade.
:::

### The loop itself

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
fichier(PARAGRAPHES, "    for k, row in enumerate(todo.itertuples(), 1)", "    res = pd.DataFrame(done)")
```

Five steps per note, and every one of them is reversible on its own: `split` cuts,
`protect` turns the `___` into integers, `translate` runs the batches, `restore` puts the
`___` back and counts what did not come back, and the pieces are re-joined with blank
lines — which reconstitutes the paragraph structure without anyone having described it.

The CSV is rewritten after **every** note. That costs milliseconds against a translation
measured in seconds, and it is what makes the ledger true at all times rather than at the
end.

The per-note line printed on the way is the whole monitoring: number of calls, characters
in and out, the length ratio, and a warning when that ratio drops below 0.7 or when a
marker was lost. Watching the first three lines is enough to know whether a run of
several hours is worth leaving alone — which is the lesson of case 5 in the appendix.

## Takeaways

- One single contract, `translate(list[str]) -> list[str]`, isolates three unrelated
  architectures. Adding or removing a translator touches one function.
- Each translator runs at its own window: the intended comparison is
  translation/English, never translator/translator.
- The three silent failure modes in this chapter — wrong architecture instantiated,
  right padding, fixed `max_new_tokens` — all produce a *plausible* output. None is
  detectable without an explicit check.
- Sorting by length makes the batch efficient; recursion on out-of-memory makes it safe.
- One element of a batch is **one paragraph**, not one note and not one sentence — 24 in
  parallel at most, and never more than the note itself holds, since `translate()` runs
  once per note.
- `main()` spends nothing on the GPU until the cheap checks have passed: the split/re-join
  round trip and the VRAM estimate both run in the first three seconds.
- The output CSV doubles as the progress ledger: resuming is free, and a finished run
  returns before the model is even loaded.
